debt.title: Let's talk about this first
debt.body: You're carrying <0>{{debt}}</0> of credit-card / consumer-loan debt. It grows at roughly <1>{{debtPct}}%</1> a year. A portfolio matching your risk profile has a long-run expectation of about <2>{{portPct}}%</2> a year — and that's an expectation, not a guarantee.
debt.ifRepay: If you clear the debt with {{amount}}
debt.repayCaption: interest you won't pay in one year — certain
debt.ifInvest: If you invest the same money
debt.investCaption: expected return in one year — not guaranteed
debt.verdict: Paying off the debt is <0>{{advantage}}</0> better for this year — with zero risk taken.
debt.covers: Your budget covers the debt; you can start investing with the remaining <0>{{leftover}}</0> with peace of mind.
debt.notCovered: Clear the debt first, then come back. Your portfolio will be waiting.
debt.assumption: The calculation assumes a card rate of {{monthly}}%/month ({{annual}}% compounded annually). This is a planning assumption, not the current official rate — the central bank revises it periodically. Check the rate on your own statement; the number shifts, the direction doesn't. You can still explore the portfolio below — it's here when you're ready.

rationale.title: Why this split?
rationale.subtitle: These weights come from a deterministic formula, not from the AI — every step is right here:
rationale.intro: Your risk score is <0>{{score}}/10</0>. The split is produced in two steps:
rationale.step1: <0>How much should stay on the safe side?</0><1/>As the risk score rises, the share of cash and bonds falls. For yours, the safe side came to <2>{{pct}}%</2> — this part cushions the shock in sharp downturns.
rationale.step2: <0>How was the remaining {{pct}}% shared out?</0><1/>Growth-side assets are weighted by their volatility (how much the price swings). At low risk scores the calm assets dominate; at high scores, the lively ones.
rationale.lowBand: Your score is on the low side, so the weight leans toward calm assets.
rationale.highBand: Your score is on the high side, so the weight leans toward lively assets.
rationale.midBand: You're in the middle, so the two are blended evenly.
rationale.droppedTitle: Why {{count}} positions? These were deliberately dropped:
rationale.footer: Your budget {{budget}} · split across at most {{cap}} assets · anything below {{minPct}}% was dropped (tiny positions are hard to track and contribute next to nothing)

reit.title: Real Estate Investing: REIT ETFs
reit.body: When your budget can't stretch to buying property outright, <0>REIT ETFs</0> let you invest in the real-estate market. They trade like stocks and hold dozens of commercial buildings and homes — you share in property returns without buying property.

XU100_IS.what: BIST 100 — an index of Türkiye's 100 largest listed companies, including giants like Turkish Airlines, Aselsan and BİM.
XU100_IS.why: As the Turkish economy grows, so does the value of these companies. The simplest way to invest in the local market.
XU100_IS.risk: Drops of 20-30% can happen in the short term. Over the long run (5+ years) the Turkish market has historically beaten inflation.

SPY.what: The S&P 500 — a basket of the 500 largest US companies. Apple, Google, Amazon and Tesla are all inside.
SPY.why: Dollar-based returns from one of the most consistently growing markets in history.
SPY.risk: It has been positive over the great majority of 10+ year windows — with exceptions: the 2000-2009 "lost decade" ended down. A long horizon usually suffices; it never guarantees.

QQQ.what: The Nasdaq 100 — a basket of the world's technology giants: Apple, Microsoft, NVIDIA, Meta and more.
QQQ.why: Tech has been the fastest-growing sector over the long run. Dollar-based, with high growth potential.
QQQ.risk: Tech stocks swing harder. Down 33% in 2022, up 55% in 2023 — it takes a strong stomach.

GLD.what: Physical gold in stock-market form. Instead of buying gold by the gram, you own a share of the dollar gold price.
GLD.why: Gold acts as a "safe haven" in crises. When stocks fall, gold often rises — it keeps your portfolio balanced.
GLD.risk: Gold doesn't grow as fast as stocks over the long run. But its power to preserve money is very high.

VNQ.what: Vanguard REIT ETF — a property basket investing in US commercial buildings, malls and housing.
VNQ.why: Even when a flat is out of budget, you can earn real-estate income with small amounts. Pays regular dividends, like rent.
VNQ.risk: Rising interest rates can weigh on property prices. And it isn't "touchable" the way physical property is.

SCHH.what: Schwab US REIT ETF — a housing-weighted American real-estate basket.
SCHH.why: Similar to VNQ but more housing-weighted. Property-market exposure with stock-like convenience.
SCHH.risk: REIT ETFs swing like stocks. But there's no buying-and-selling-property hassle, and you can cash out instantly.

VXUS.what: Vanguard Total International Stock — companies in every developed and emerging market EXCEPT the United States.
VXUS.why: Stops your portfolio from being a bet on one country. When the US lags, the rest of the world often does not.
VXUS.risk: Currency moves cut both ways, and emerging markets swing harder than developed ones.

EXS1_DE.what: iShares Core DAX — the 40 largest listed companies in Germany: SAP, Siemens, Allianz and the rest.
EXS1_DE.why: Your home market, in one purchase, priced in the currency you earn and spend in.
EXS1_DE.risk: Forty companies in one country, heavy on industry and exports. A German downturn hits all of it at once.

IUSA_DE.what: iShares S&P 500 UCITS — the 500 largest US companies, in a fund that EU investors are allowed to buy.
IUSA_DE.why: The same exposure as the famous US index funds, in a wrapper that is legal for you. EU rules bar US-domiciled ETFs from retail investors.
IUSA_DE.risk: One country, and one currency you do not earn in: a falling dollar eats returns even when the index rises.

EUNL_DE.what: iShares Core MSCI World — roughly 1,500 large companies across 23 developed countries, in one fund.
EUNL_DE.why: The simplest way to stop guessing which country wins. If you hold one stock fund, this is the usual candidate.
EUNL_DE.risk: "World" is misleading: it is about 70% United States, and it holds no emerging markets at all.

4GLD_DE.what: Xetra-Gold — a security backed by physical gold held in a Frankfurt vault, which you can in principle demand delivery of.
4GLD_DE.why: When stocks fall, gold often does not. It is the ballast rather than the engine.
4GLD_DE.risk: It pays no interest and no dividend. Over long stretches it can simply sit still while everything else moves.

IQQP_DE.what: iShares European Property Yield — listed property companies across Europe, paying out their rental income.
IQQP_DE.why: Property exposure in euros, without a mortgage, a notary, or 7% in purchase costs before you own anything.
IQQP_DE.risk: Listed property moves with the stock market in a crash, exactly when you hoped it would not. Rate rises hurt it twice.

XEON_DE.what: Xtrackers Overnight Rate Swap — tracks the euro overnight rate. As close to "cash that earns something" as a fund gets.
XEON_DE.why: Where the calm part of the portfolio waits. Reachable in a day, and not exposed to the stock market at all.
XEON_DE.risk: It follows the central bank's rate. When that rate is below inflation, you are losing purchasing power quietly.

EUNA_DE.what: iShares Core Euro Government Bond — loans to euro-area governments, held in one fund.
EUNA_DE.why: The traditional counterweight to stocks: when shares fall in a panic, government bonds are what people buy instead.
EUNA_DE.risk: 2022 showed the counterweight can fail — stocks and bonds fell together when rates rose fast. Longer bonds fall hardest.

stocks.what: An ownership share of a company or a basket of companies. As the business grows, so does your share.
stocks.why: The asset class with the highest long-run returns — growth potential well above inflation.
stocks.risk: Sharp short-term drops happen. Recovery has historically come most of the time, but it can take years.

gold.what: A precious metal that has held value for millennia. Known as "crisis insurance".
gold.why: When stocks fall, gold often rises. It helps your portfolio keep its balance.
gold.risk: It won't earn like stocks over the long run, but it stops your money from melting away.

fund.what: A pooled investment managed by professionals on your behalf, bought and sold through fund platforms.
fund.why: No need to pick individual stocks — experts manage the mix for you.
fund.risk: Management fees are deducted, and performance depends on the manager's decisions.

reit.what: A basket of income-producing property — offices, warehouses, housing — that you can buy a slice of on an exchange.
reit.why: Real-estate exposure without needing the price of a flat, and without a title deed to manage. The rent arrives as dividends.
reit.risk: Rising interest rates weigh on property values. And it is not "touchable" the way a flat you own is.

cash.what: Money parked in very short-term, very safe instruments. It is the part of your portfolio that does not move.
cash.why: It is what lets you sleep, and what you spend in an emergency instead of selling stocks at the worst possible moment.
cash.risk: The safest thing in nominal terms, and a slow loss in real terms: it rarely keeps pace with inflation.

bond.what: A basket of loans to governments and large companies. They pay you interest and return the principal at the end.
bond.why: It usually moves less than stocks, and often in the other direction, which softens the whole portfolio's swings.
bond.risk: When interest rates rise, existing bonds fall in price. Lower long-run return than stocks, by design.

guide.title: First Investment Guide
guide.subtitle: Broker → Deposit → First order, step by step for {{market}}

1.title: What Is a Broker?
1.body: To buy and sell stocks and funds you need a brokerage account. It's like a bank account, but for investing. Anyone operating one legally in {{market}} is licensed by {{regulator}} — check that before you send a single unit of currency, and check it on the regulator's own site rather than the broker's.

2.title: How Do I Open an Account?
2.body:
1. Go to your chosen broker's site.
2. Start the account opening.
3. Give your identity details — {{market}} will have its own requirement, usually a national identity number or tax number.
4. Verify who you are, by video call, by post or in a branch.
5. It is usually live within a few business days.

3.title: How Do I Deposit Money?
3.body: Transfer from a bank account in YOUR OWN NAME. A broker that accepts money from someone else's account, or asks you to send it to a personal account rather than a corporate one, is a broker to walk away from.

4.title: How Do I Place the First Order?
4.body:
1. Find "Buy" or "Place order".
2. Search for the asset.
3. Enter the amount.
4. Choose a market order — it fills at the current price.
5. Confirm.

The first one will feel like a bigger moment than it is. Keep it small enough that it does not.

5.title: Tracking and Patience
5.body: After buying, don't build a habit of checking daily — it feeds anxiety and changes nothing. Once a week is plenty. Lumos will tell you about the moves that actually matter.

advisor.greeting:
Lumos Advisor.

Ask anything on your mind about investing or this app, in your own words — you're not limited to the canned questions. I explain concepts, walk you through the reasoning behind a portfolio decision, and put news in context.

One boundary: I won't say "buy" or "sell" for any specific stock or fund, and I won't predict where the market is going — nobody can honestly know those. Beyond that, nothing is off limits.

etf.title: An ETF Is Really a Basket
etf.body: One purchase makes you part-owner of dozens of stocks. No picking them one by one — investing, pre-packaged.

diversification.title: Don't Put All Your Eggs in One Basket
diversification.body: Spread across different assets and one bad day can't take everything. That's called diversification.

inflation.title: Inflation Melts Your Money
inflation.body: At 50% inflation, 100 under the mattress behaves like 67 a year later. Not investing is a risk too.

dividend.title: A Dividend Is Like Rent
dividend.body: Your share of the company's profit. It pays you regularly for as long as you hold the stock — like renting out property.

reel-return.title: Real Return Is the True Gain
reel-return.body: You made 45% but inflation was 60%? You actually lost. Always look at the inflation-adjusted return.

liquidity.title: Liquidity Saves You
liquidity.body: Stocks turn to cash in minutes; land can take months. You might need money urgently — don't forget that.

drawdown.title: Drops Are Normal
drawdown.body: Markets often fall 10-15%. That's not panic, it's the natural cycle. No loss is locked in unless you sell.

gold.title: Gold Is Like Insurance
gold.body: In crises, gold usually rises while stocks fall. Think of it as your portfolio's "protective shield".

patience.title: Patience Is the Best Strategy
patience.body: The great majority of 10-year windows in S&P 500 history have been positive — though periods like 2000-2009 lost money. Time is your strongest tool, not a guarantee.

reit.title: Be a Landlord Without Buying a House
reit.body: REIT ETFs let you earn real-estate income with small amounts. A way to be a property investor without buying property.

fomo.title: FOMO Is Your Enemy
fomo.body: "Everyone's buying, so I will too" is the most dangerous sentence in investing. Buy every rally and you'll usually catch the top.

cost-avg.title: Regular Investing Lowers Risk
cost-avg.body: Investing the same amount monthly means buying cheap some months and dear in others. The result: a below-average cost.

goal.title: 🎯 My Goal
goal.subtitle: Let's turn a goal like "a house deposit in 3 years" into a concrete monthly plan.
goal.monthlyPlaceholder: How much do you save monthly right now? (opt.)
goal.alreadyOnTrack: Your existing savings reach the goal on their own — no extra contribution needed.
goal.needMonthly: To reach the goal on time you need to save about <0>{{amount}}</0> a month.
goal.realValueNote: Assuming {{inflation}}% inflation, your {{target}} goal will be worth ≈ <0>{{real}}</0> in today's money by then. A fixed target loses purchasing power over time — you may want to revisit it.
goal.onTrack: ✓ You're reaching the goal on time.
goal.delayed: At this pace your goal slips by about <0>{{months}} months</0>.
goal.howTitle: What is this calculation based on?
goal.howBody: It assumes the money you save doesn't sit idle but grows in a portfolio matching your risk profile, at an average {{growth}}% a year. That rate isn't invented: it's live inflation ({{inflation}}%) plus the real premium a diversified portfolio is assumed to earn over the long run. The horizon is converted to {{months}} months, and each contribution's growth over the remaining time is counted.
goal.howFormula: monthly = (target − grown value of current savings) × r / ((1+r)^months − 1),  r = monthly return
goal.howCaveat: This is a planning assumption, not a forecast: markets don't grow the same amount every year, and some years close down. If the rate turns out lower, the monthly figure won't be enough — reviewing the plan once a year is a good habit.

headlines.progress: {{seen}}/{{total}} headlines decoded · tap the card → next one

headline-crash.headline: 📰 "THE MARKET CRASHED"
headline-crash.reality: The index most likely fell 2–4%. Historically such drops have usually been recovered within months. "Crash" is attractive for a headline and ordinary for an investor.
headline-crash.action: Stay calm. Selling today turns the drop into a real loss.

headline-crash-global.headline: 📰 "A CRISIS IS COMING"
headline-crash-global.reality: Crisis predictions are constant in the media — most never arrive. After the ones that did, markets have historically recovered, though it can take years.
headline-crash-global.action: Prepare with diversification, not with panic.

headline-gold.headline: 📰 "GOLD HITS A RECORD"
headline-gold.reality: Gold rising usually means uncertainty is around. It does not mean your other assets became worthless — different assets shine in different conditions.
headline-gold.action: Depending on one asset is risky. Balance matters.

headline-dolar.headline: 📰 "THE DOLLAR IS SURGING"
headline-dolar.reality: When the local currency weakens, the local value of FX-based assets rises. If your portfolio holds some, this headline may be protecting you.
headline-dolar.action: Hold some FX-based assets to balance currency risk.

rvb.subtitle: We compare the same home two ways: buying with a down payment plus a mortgage, or renting and investing the difference. Buying is not always the win.

rvb.assumptions: Assumptions: housing +{{housing}}%/yr, portfolio +{{portfolio}}%/yr, mortgage {{rate}}%/yr {{rateSource}} ({{term}}-year term), inflation {{inflation}}%/yr (data through {{asOf}}). Purchase costs are included: transfer taxes and official fees {{deed}}% + agency commission {{agency}}% + VAT ({{vat}}%) = {{agencyVat}}%; plus {{upkeep}}% of the home's value per year for dues, insurance and upkeep. These rates are set by regulation and custom and change over time. Large figures are inflated mostly by inflation; the "in today's money" line shows the real value. The calculation assumes you keep living in the home, so taxes arising on a sale and the non-financial value of owning are excluded — the emotional side of that decision is legitimate too.

sections.p: Lumos stores what you tell it about your money so it can give you the same answer tomorrow. It does not sell your data, does not run advertising, and does not track you across other sites. You can delete everything from inside the app, and the deletion is real.

Your sign-in identity — email address and name — is held by Clerk, our authentication provider, and your email is copied into our database so the app can tell accounts apart.

Your risk profile: the answers you give during onboarding — age, monthly income, savings rate, investment horizon, loss tolerance, experience, goal, income stability, and any high-interest debt you report — plus the risk score derived from them.

Your holdings: for each asset you add, its type, name, ticker, purchase date and amount, currency, quantity, any current value you enter by hand, your note, and the optional emotion tag.

Your choices: chosen market, chosen language, investment path, and the fear you picked at check-in.

Anything you write in the feedback box, together with the page you were on.

No payment card details, bank credentials, national identity numbers or brokerage logins — the app never asks for them, and you should never enter them. No advertising identifiers, no third-party tracking pixels, no cross-site profiling. Lumos cannot see or touch any real brokerage account; everything you enter is a record you typed, not a connection to your money.

The database is hosted by Neon in Frankfurt, Germany (eu-central-1). The application server runs on Render in Oregon, United States, which means your data is processed in the United States as well as stored in the EU. The web app is served by Vercel. Authentication is handled by Clerk.

sections.h: What is sent to the AI models
sections.p: When you use the advisor, your message is sent to an AI provider — Google Gemini, Groq or OpenRouter, depending on availability — together with the parts of your profile and portfolio needed to answer sensibly. Your name and email address are not included. These providers process the request under their own terms; Lumos uses their free tiers, and free tiers commonly permit the provider to use submitted content to improve their services. Treat the advisor as a public conversation: do not paste anything into it you would not want a third party to hold.

If error monitoring is enabled, Sentry receives technical details of a crash — the error, the code path, the request id. It is configured with personal information disabled, so your profile answers and holdings are not attached to error reports.

sections.h: What is kept in your browser
sections.p: Lumos stores your chosen language and market, and a cached copy of the market list, in your browser so the app opens the way you left it. Clerk sets the cookies needed to keep you signed in. There are no advertising or analytics cookies.

Your data is kept for as long as your account exists. Market data caches are technical and hold no personal information. Delete your account and the data goes with it — there is no retention period afterwards, and no archived copy waiting to be restored.

Profile → Delete my account. It removes your profile, every holding, and every piece of feedback you submitted from our database, and then deletes your login from Clerk so the account cannot be signed into again. It is immediate and cannot be undone. If the login removal fails for any reason, the app tells you so rather than claiming success.

You can see everything Lumos holds about you inside the app — that is all of it; there is no hidden profile. You can correct it by editing it, and you can erase it with the deletion above. If you are in the EU or UK, the GDPR rights of access, rectification, erasure, restriction, portability and objection apply, and you may complain to your national data protection authority. Email dilaydikbiyik@gmail.com for anything the app itself cannot do.
Lumos is not intended for anyone under 18 and is not directed at children.
If this policy changes in a way that affects what is collected or who receives it, the date at the top changes and the change is noted in the app's release notes.

Lumos is an educational tool for people who are new to investing. It explains concepts, shows what official data says, and lets you rehearse decisions — including with play money — before any real money is involved.

It is not investment advice, financial advice, tax advice or legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a licensed professional. Lumos is not authorised or regulated by the SPK, the SEC, FINRA, BaFin or any other financial authority. Nothing in the app is a recommendation to buy or sell any particular security, fund or property. Lumos cannot execute a trade, hold your money, or access any account you hold elsewhere.

Figures come from official sources — the Turkish central bank, the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, the St. Louis Fed, Eurostat and the Deutsche Bundesbank — and from market data providers. They can be delayed, revised or simply unavailable, and the app says so when it is showing you something old.

Projections are not forecasts. They are arithmetic applied to stated assumptions, and the assumptions are printed underneath every result precisely so you can disagree with them. Transfer taxes, agency commission, VAT and upkeep rates are set by regulation and custom and they change; verify them against the current rules before treating any output as a decision.
Every historical figure in the app describes what already happened. It does not indicate what will happen next. You can lose money investing, including more than you expected to.
Decisions you make are yours. The accuracy of what you type — your income, your holdings, your debt — determines the usefulness of what comes back, and Lumos has no way to verify any of it.

Keep your sign-in secure and do not share it. Use Lumos lawfully: no attempts to break, overload or reverse the service, no scraping, and no using it to advise other people as though it were a licensed service. The free AI tier is subject to a daily message limit. We may suspend an account that is being used to attack or abuse the service.

Lumos is provided as-is, with no guarantee of availability or of uninterrupted operation. It depends on third-party data and AI providers that can fail or change their terms; features may change or be withdrawn.

To the extent the law allows, Lumos and its author are not liable for investment losses, lost profits, or any indirect or consequential loss arising from use of the app or from reliance on anything it displays. Nothing here limits liability that cannot lawfully be limited.
These terms may change; the date at the top shows when they last did. Continuing to use Lumos after a change means you accept it. Questions: dilaydikbiyik@gmail.com.

rvbEmotion.title: The part that isn't a number
rvbEmotion.body:
Everything above is arithmetic, and arithmetic is only half of this decision. Owning where you live buys something a spreadsheet cannot price: not being asked to leave, being allowed to paint a wall, knowing what next year's housing costs are. People who have moved because a landlord decided to sell know exactly what that is worth.

It cuts the other way too. A home ties you to one city, and a job you would otherwise take somewhere else becomes a much bigger decision.

If the numbers are close, this is the part that should settle it — and if the numbers are far apart, it is worth knowing which way you are leaning before you look for reasons.
